course.title: JavaScript Canvas Game Development Mastery
course.description: A comprehensive 40-part course taking you from absolute beginner to confident game developer using HTML5 Canvas and JavaScript. Covers Canvas API fundamentals, game loops, physics, animation, collision detection, sprite systems, particle effects, sound, AI, and complete architectural design of 4 full games: Pong, Flappy Bird, Platformer, and Space Shooter.

blocks.value: Welcome to Canvas Game Development

HTML5 Canvas is a powerful drawing API that lets you render graphics, animations, and entire games directly in the browser using JavaScript. Unlike DOM-based games, Canvas gives you pixel-level control over every frame — making it the industry standard for 2D web games.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing browser window with Canvas element rendering game graphics via JavaScript
blocks.caption: Canvas acts as a blank slate that JavaScript paints onto every frame

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Infographic/Diagram — A browser window showing a Canvas element in the center. Arrows show: JavaScript code → Canvas 2D Context → Rendered graphics (shapes, sprites, text). Include browser UI (URL bar, tabs) to ground it in reality. Use modern flat design with Canvas blue (#E44D26) and JS yellow (#F7DF1E) colors.
Why Canvas for Games?

• **Pixel-perfect control** — draw anything, not limited by HTML/CSS
• **60 FPS rendering** — hardware-accelerated 2D graphics
• **No DOM overhead** — thousands of sprites without lag
• **Cross-platform** — works on desktop, mobile, and tablets
• **Industry standard** — used by Phaser, PixiJS, and major game engines

blocks.alt: Comparison showing DOM-based game lagging vs Canvas game running smoothly with many sprites
blocks.caption: Canvas handles thousands of moving objects where the DOM struggles

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Split Comparison — Left: DOM game with 100 div elements, choppy FPS counter in red (15 FPS). Right: Canvas game with 1000 particles, smooth FPS counter in green (60 FPS). Use performance graphs or simple visual metaphors. Label 'DOM Limitations' vs 'Canvas Power'.
The Rendering Pipeline

Every Canvas game follows a loop: Clear the canvas → Update game state → Draw everything → Repeat. This happens 60 times per second. The browser calls your draw function via requestAnimationFrame() for smooth, synchronized rendering.

blocks.output: A blue rectangle with white text 'Hello, Canvas!' rendered on the canvas

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of HTML5 Canvas?
options: To style web pages with CSS
To draw graphics and animations via JavaScript
blocks.correctAnswer: To draw graphics and animations via JavaScript
blocks.explanation: Canvas is a drawing surface controlled entirely by JavaScript. It has no styling capabilities of its own — everything is rendered programmatically.

blocks.question: Which method gets the drawing context for 2D graphics?
blocks.explanation: getContext('2d') returns the CanvasRenderingContext2D object, which provides all drawing methods like fillRect, strokeRect, and arc.

blocks.question: What HTML tag is used to create a canvas element?
blocks.explanation: The <canvas> tag creates the drawing surface in HTML. You must then use JavaScript to actually draw on it.

parts.partTitle: Part 2: Setting Up Your Development Environment

blocks.value: Your Game Dev Workspace

Before building games, you need a solid development environment. We'll use VS Code (free, fast, excellent JavaScript support), a local server (for module imports), and browser DevTools for debugging. No frameworks yet — pure Canvas and vanilla JS.

blocks.alt: VS Code editor showing Canvas game project with Live Server extension running
blocks.caption: VS Code with Live Server is the recommended setup for Canvas development

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — VS Code window showing a project with index.html, game.js, and styles.css files in the sidebar. The editor shows a Canvas setup. The bottom status bar shows 'Live Server: Port 5500'. Dark theme preferred. Include the Live Server extension icon highlighted.
Project Structure

Organize your game project from day one. A clean folder structure prevents chaos as your game grows:

📁 my-canvas-game/
├── 📄 index.html
├── 📄 styles.css
├── 📁 js/
│   ├── 📄 main.js
│   ├── 📄 game.js
│   └── 📄 utils.js
└── 📁 assets/
    ├── 📁 images/
    ├── 📁 audio/
    └── 📁 fonts/

blocks.alt: File explorer showing organized game project folder structure
blocks.caption: A well-organized project scales from prototype to production

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: File Tree Diagram — Clean tree structure showing folders and files. Use folder icons (yellow) and file icons (white with extensions). Color-code by type: HTML (orange), CSS (blue), JS (yellow), assets (green). Include a small note: 'Start simple, grow organized'.

<!-- index.html -- Your game's entry point -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>My Canvas Game</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
    <!-- The canvas where magic happens -->
    <canvas id="gameCanvas"></canvas>
    
    <!-- Load game logic -->
    <script type="module" src="js/main.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
blocks.output: A blank HTML page with a canvas element ready for drawing

blocks.value: CSS for Full-Screen Canvas
Use CSS to make your canvas fill the screen and remove default margins. The canvas will maintain its internal resolution while stretching to fit the window.

blocks.output: Full-screen centered canvas with dark background and subtle border

blocks.value: JavaScript Module Setup
Using ES6 modules (type="module") keeps your code organized. Each file handles one responsibility: main.js bootstraps, game.js runs the loop, utils.js holds helpers.

blocks.output: Game instance created and started when page loads
A red square animating smoothly at 60 FPS on a dark background

blocks.question: Why do we use type="module" in the script tag?
options: To make the code run faster
blocks.explanation: type="module" tells the browser to treat the script as an ES6 module, allowing import/export statements for clean code organization.

blocks.question: What CSS property prevents scrollbars when canvas is full-screen?
blocks.explanation: overflow: hidden on the body element prevents scrollbars from appearing when the canvas fills the viewport.

blocks.question: Which HTML attribute on <script> enables ES6 module imports?
blocks.explanation: The type="module" attribute is required to use import/export syntax in browser JavaScript without a bundler.

parts.partTitle: Part 3: The Canvas 2D Context — Drawing Primitives

blocks.value: Drawing Shapes and Paths

The Canvas 2D Context (ctx) is your paintbrush. It provides methods to draw rectangles, circles, lines, curves, and text. Master these primitives — they are the building blocks of every game object you'll ever create.

blocks.alt: Canvas showing various shapes: filled rect, stroked circle, line path, arc, and text
blocks.caption: Canvas primitives: rectangles, circles, lines, arcs, and text

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Reference Sheet — A canvas with labeled examples: 'fillRect' (blue filled rectangle), 'strokeRect' (red outlined rectangle), 'arc' (green circle), 'lineTo' (purple zigzag path), 'fillText' (orange text). Each with a small arrow and label. Clean, educational style with a grid background.
Rectangles and Colors
The simplest shapes to draw. fillRect() draws a solid rectangle; strokeRect() draws just the outline. Set colors using fillStyle and strokeStyle before drawing.

blocks.output: A red filled rectangle, a blue outlined rectangle, and a transparent rectangle cutout

blocks.value: Circles and Arcs
Use arc() for circles and arcs. The angles are in radians, not degrees. Math.PI = 180°, so a full circle is Math.PI * 2.

blocks.output: A full orange circle and a yellow pac-man shape

blocks.value: Paths and Lines
For custom shapes, use paths: beginPath() starts a new shape, moveTo() positions the pen, lineTo() draws lines, and closePath() connects back to the start.

blocks.output: A purple triangle and a golden star drawn with path commands

blocks.value: Text Rendering
Display scores, health bars, and UI text. Use fillText() for solid text and strokeText() for outlined text. The font property accepts CSS font syntax.

blocks.output: White 'Score: 1000' text and red outlined 'GAME OVER' text on canvas

blocks.value: State Stack: Save and Restore
Canvas drawing state (colors, transforms, clipping) can be saved and restored. This is crucial for nested drawing operations and preventing style leaks.

blocks.output: Two rectangles: one translated to (100,100) in red, one at (0,0) in default black

blocks.question: What unit does Canvas use for angles in arc()?
blocks.explanation: Canvas uses radians for all angle measurements. Math.PI is 180°, so a full circle is Math.PI * 2.

blocks.question: Which method starts a new path for drawing custom shapes?
blocks.explanation: beginPath() clears the current path and starts a new one. Without it, new lines connect to the previous path's end point.

blocks.question: Which property sets the color used by fillRect() and fill()?
blocks.explanation: fillStyle sets the color, gradient, or pattern used for filling shapes. It must be set BEFORE calling fill() or fillRect().

parts.partTitle: Part 4: The Game Loop and Delta Time

blocks.value: The Heartbeat of Every Game

The game loop is the most important concept in game development. It runs continuously, updating game state and rendering frames. A well-designed loop runs at 60 FPS (frames per second) and remains smooth even when the browser is busy.

blocks.alt: Circular diagram showing game loop: Process Input → Update → Draw → Repeat
blocks.caption: The game loop: process input, update state, render frame, repeat forever

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Circular Flowchart — A large circle divided into three segments with arrows: 1) 'Process Input' (keyboard/mouse icon, blue), 2) 'Update State' (gear icon, green), 3) 'Render Frame' (monitor icon, red). Arrows flow clockwise with '60x/second' label. Center shows a clock face. Clean, modern design.
requestAnimationFrame
Never use setInterval for games! requestAnimationFrame() syncs with the monitor's refresh rate, pauses in background tabs (saving battery), and provides a timestamp for calculating delta time.

blocks.output: Smooth 60 FPS game loop running continuously

blocks.value: Delta Time: Frame-Independent Movement
Without delta time, your game runs at different speeds on different computers. Multiply all movement by deltaTime so objects move at consistent speeds regardless of frame rate.

blocks.alt: Comparison showing object moving same distance in 1 second at 30 FPS vs 60 FPS using delta time
blocks.caption: Delta time ensures consistent speed across all frame rates

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Comparison Diagram — Top timeline: 30 FPS (frames spaced far apart). Bottom timeline: 60 FPS (frames close together). Both show a ball moving from left to right, ending at the same position after 1 second. Label 'Without dt: Ball moves slower at 30 FPS' (red X) vs 'With dt: Same speed at any FPS' (green check). Use distance markers.

blocks.output: Player moves at exactly 200 pixels/second on any monitor

blocks.value: FPS Counter
Monitor your game's performance with a real-time FPS counter. If FPS drops below 60, you know your update or draw functions are too heavy.

blocks.output: Green 'FPS: 60' text displayed in the top-left corner of canvas

blocks.value: Fixed Time Steps for Physics
For stable physics (collision detection, velocity calculations), use a fixed time step. Update physics at a constant rate (e.g., 60Hz) while rendering as fast as possible.

blocks.output: Physics simulation running at fixed 60Hz with smooth variable-FPS rendering

blocks.question: Why should you use requestAnimationFrame instead of setInterval?
options: It syncs with monitor refresh and saves battery
blocks.correctAnswer: It syncs with monitor refresh and saves battery
blocks.explanation: requestAnimationFrame matches the monitor's refresh rate, pauses in background tabs, and provides timestamps for delta time calculations.

blocks.question: What does delta time (dt) represent?
options: The total game time in seconds
Time elapsed since the last frame in seconds
The number of frames per second
blocks.correctAnswer: Time elapsed since the last frame in seconds
blocks.explanation: Delta time is the duration between the current frame and the previous frame, measured in seconds. It makes movement frame-rate independent.

blocks.question: Which method schedules the next frame and provides a timestamp?
blocks.explanation: requestAnimationFrame(callback) schedules the browser to call your function before the next repaint, passing a high-resolution timestamp.

parts.partTitle: Part 5: Keyboard and Mouse Input Handling

blocks.value: Capturing Player Input

Games are interactive. You need to detect when players press keys, move the mouse, or click. Canvas doesn't have built-in input — you listen to browser events and track the state yourself. A clean input manager is essential for responsive controls.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing keyboard and mouse events flowing into an Input Manager that updates game state
blocks.caption: Input events flow through a manager that tracks current key and mouse states

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Flow Diagram — Left side: Keyboard (key icon) and Mouse (cursor icon) sending events. Center: 'InputManager' box with internal state maps (keysDown, mousePos). Right: Game objects reading from InputManager. Arrows show event flow. Use blue for keyboard, orange for mouse, green for manager.
Keyboard State Tracking
Don't check events inside your game loop! Instead, maintain a state object that tracks which keys are currently pressed. Check this state during update().

blocks.output: Responsive keyboard controls with support for held keys and single-press actions

blocks.value: Mouse Position and Clicks
Get mouse coordinates relative to the canvas (not the window). Handle clicks, movement, and button states for aiming, shooting, and UI interaction.

blocks.output: Mouse tracking relative to canvas with click detection

blocks.value: Touch Input for Mobile
Mobile games use touch events. Map touchstart, touchmove, and touchend to your input system. Prevent default to stop page scrolling.

blocks.output: Multi-touch input support for mobile devices

blocks.value: Common Key Codes Reference
Modern JavaScript uses e.code (physical key) instead of e.keyCode (deprecated). Here are the most common game controls:

blocks.output: Clean, maintainable control mapping using e.code values

blocks.value: Input Buffering
Input buffering stores recent inputs for a short time. This makes controls feel responsive — e.g., pressing jump 50ms before landing still registers.

blocks.output: Jump input buffered for 100ms, making controls feel more forgiving

blocks.question: Why track key states instead of handling events directly in the game loop?
options: Events are unpredictable; state polling is reliable
blocks.correctAnswer: Events are unpredictable; state polling is reliable
blocks.explanation: Events fire asynchronously. By storing key states, you can check them predictably during your update() function every frame.

blocks.question: Which property gives the physical key location regardless of keyboard layout?
blocks.explanation: e.code returns the physical key location (e.g., 'KeyW', 'ArrowLeft'), making controls consistent across different keyboard layouts and languages.

blocks.question: Which event prevents default touch scrolling on mobile?
blocks.explanation: Calling e.preventDefault() in touch event handlers stops the browser from scrolling the page, keeping the game in control.
